questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman has had increased malaise for 3 weeks and decreased urine output. Urinalysis shows protein 1+ and blood 3+. Urine microscopic analysis shows RBC casts. Her serum creatinine is 4.3 mg/dL. A renal biopsy is performed, and immunofluorescence microscopy shows a granular pattern of staining with antibody to C3. Which of the following types of hypersensitivity reactions is most likely causing her renal disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Type III (Immune complex formation)

 

This patient's presentation suggests glomerulonephritis, specifically a nephritic syndrome, characterized by:

 

  • Hematuria (3+ blood)
  • RBC casts in urine
  • Proteinuria
  • Elevated serum creatinine
  • Granular immunofluorescence pattern with C3

 

Type III hypersensitivity involves:

 

  • Formation of antigen-antibody immune complexes
  • Deposition in tissues (e.g., glomerular basement membrane)
  • Activation of complement (e.g., C3), leading to inflammation and tissue injury

 

The granular IF pattern (not linear) is classic for immune complex glomerulonephritis, seen in:

 

  • Post-streptococcal GN
  • Lupus nephritis
  • Membranoproliferative GN
  • IgA nephropathy (in some cases)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Type I (IgE-mediated systemic anaphylaxis): Seen in allergies/anaphylaxis, not immune complex GN.

 

Option B.  Type II (Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity): Involves antibodies directed against cell surface antigens (e.g., in Goodpasture’s syndrome, which shows a linear IF pattern, not granular).

 

Option D. Type IV (Delayed-type hypersensitivity): T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity — e.g., in contact dermatitis, TB — not typical for this renal pathology.

questions.stem: A study of renal disease identifies patients with greater than 3.5 g of protein in a 24-hour urine collection, but no RBCs or WBCs. Dysfunction involving which of the following cells is most likely to be responsible for proteinuria?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Podocytes

 

This patient is described as having nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), with no hematuria or pyuria. This points to a nephrotic syndrome.

 

Podocytes:

 

  • Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells that line the outer layer of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
  • They have foot processes that interdigitate and form filtration slits with slit diaphragms — crucial for the size and charge selectivity of the glomerular filtration barrier.

 

Why podocyte dysfunction leads to proteinuria:

 

  • When podocytes are damaged or effaced (as in minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, etc.), the filtration barrier becomes leaky.
  • Large proteins (e.g., albumin) leak into the urine → proteinuria.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Endothelium: Damage here typically leads to hematuria and inflammation, seen more in nephritic syndrome.

 

Option B. Macula densa: Part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, regulates glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and renin release, not filtration barrier integrity.

 

Option C. Mesangium: Involved in structural support and immune complex clearance; damage here can cause inflammation and hematuria, again more common in nephritic syndromes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Proteinuria in the nephrotic range without hematuria or inflammation points to podocyte injury, which is key in nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old previously healthy man has noticed blood in his urine for the past 2 days Laboratory findings show a serum urea nitrogen level of 39 mg/dL and creatinine level of 4.1 mg/dL. A renal biopsy specimen is obtained; the immunofluorescence pattern of staining with antibody against human IgG is shown in the figure. Which of the following serologic findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody

 

The image and clinical vignette describe a classic case of Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease):

 

  • Young male (21 years old) with hematuria (blood in urine) and acute kidney injury (elevated BUN and creatinine).
  • Renal biopsy shows linear immunofluorescence staining with IgG - visible in the image provided. 

 

The question asks for the most likely serologic finding.

 

Diagnosis:

 

  • Goodpasture syndrome, which is caused by autoantibodies against the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
  • The characteristic linear pattern of IgG deposition along the GBM on immunofluorescence is diagnostic.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Anti-streptolysin O antibody: Seen in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which typically shows granular ("lumpy-bumpy") deposits.

 

Option C. C3 nephritic factor: Associated with dense deposit disease (MPGN type II), not Goodpasture’s.

 

Option D. Hepatitis B surface antigen antibody: Seen in some cases of membranous nephropathy, not anti-GBM disease.

questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is found to have mild hypertension. Laboratory findings show a serum creatinine level of 2.2 mg/dL Microalbuminuria is present, A renal biopsy is done; the light microscopic appearance of a PAS- stained specimen is shown in the figure. Blood test for which of the following is most likely to be abnormal in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hemoglobin A1c

 

Clinical Scenario Breakdown:

 

  • 58-year-old man with mild hypertension
  • Serum creatinine: 2.2 mg/dL (elevated)
  • Microalbuminuria (early sign of kidney damage)

 

PAS-stained renal biopsy image shows glomerular basement membrane thickening and nodular mesangial expansion (classic Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules)

 

Histological Interpretation:

 

The image and description strongly point toward diabetic nephropathy, a chronic complication of diabetes mellitus.

 

Supporting Features:

 

  • The PAS stain highlights thickened capillary basement membranes and mesangial matrix expansion.
  • These findings are characteristic of diabetic nephropathy, especially the nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules).
  • Hemoglobin A1c reflects long-term glycemic control, and it would be elevated in patients with poorly controlled diabetes - the root cause of diabetic nephropathy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anti–glomerular basement membrane antibody: Seen in Goodpasture syndrome, which presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and often pulmonary symptoms, not chronic microalbuminuria.

 

Option B: Antinuclear antibody: Associated with lupus nephritis, which has different histopathological findings (wire loops, full-house immunofluorescence).

 

Option C. Anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody: Seen in vasculitides like granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis, not in diabetic nephropathy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The renal biopsy findings and clinical data are most consistent with diabetic nephropathy, making Hemoglobin A1c the most relevant and likely abnormal lab test.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is involved in a motor vehicle accident and develops oliguria and dark brown urine. The urine dipstick analysis is positive for myoglobin and for blood, but microscopic examination of the urine shows no RBCs. Which of the following renal lesions was most likely present in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. B. Acute tubular injury

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with acute myelogenous leukemia After induction with a multiagent chemotherapy protocol, he has an episode of lower abdominal pain accompanied by passage of red urine. Which of the following urinalysis findings is most likely to be reported for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Uric acid crystals

 

This 28-year-old man with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) who develops lower abdominal pain and red urine after chemotherapy is most likely experiencing tumor lysis syndrome (TLS).

 

Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS):

 

  • Occurs after rapid lysis of malignant cells, especially after chemotherapy in leukemias and lymphomas.
  • Massive release of intracellular contents into bloodstream:
  • ↑ Uric acid
  • ↑ Potassium
  • ↑ Phosphate
  • ↓ Calcium

 

High uric acid → precipitates in renal tubules, causing:

 

  • Red or tea-colored urine
  • Renal colic/lower abdominal pain
  • Acute kidney injury

 

Urinalysis in TLS:

 

  • Uric acid crystals are typically present.
  • The urine may be acidic and contain these crystals, which may appear reddish or brownish.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bence Jones protein: Seen in multiple myeloma, not AML.

 

Option B. Eosinophils: Seen in allergic interstitial nephritis, not typical in AML or TLS.

 

Option C. Myoglobin: Seen in rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown leads to myoglobinuria. No history of trauma or muscle injury here.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl develops cramping abdominal pain and diarrhea. She has decreased urine output. A stool sample is positive for occult blood. The peripheral blood smear shows schistocytes, and the serum D-dimer level is elevated. A renal biopsy speci- men shows small thrombi within glomerular capillary loops. This complication develops most commonly after infection with which of the following organisms?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. Escherichia coli

questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D. Collecting duct carcinoma

questions.stem: A student is studying the glomerular slit diaphragm closely. He observes that there is a transmembrane protein “X” with a large extracellular portion made up of immunoglobulin (Ig)-like domains. The ‘X’ molecules extend toward each other from neighboring foot processes and dimerize across the slit diaphragm. Identify the “X”?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Nephrin

 

1. Structure and Function of the Glomerular Slit Diaphragm

 

  • The slit diaphragm is a specialized structure found between the foot processes (also known as pedicels) of podocytes in the kidney glomerulus.
  • It acts as a critical filtration barrier, preventing proteins from leaking into the urine.

 

2. Clues from the Question

 

  • "Transmembrane protein ‘X’": This protein spans the membrane of podocyte foot processes.
  • "Large extracellular portion made up of immunoglobulin (Ig)-like domains": This describes a protein motif common in cell adhesion molecules.

 

"‘X’ molecules extend toward each other from neighboring foot processes and dimerize across the slit diaphragm": The protein forms bridges between podocytes, essential for slit diaphragm structure.

 

3. Why Nephrin?

 

  • Nephrin perfectly fits all these features! It is a transmembrane protein with a significant extracellular region containing immunoglobulin-like domains.
  • On each side of the slit diaphragm, nephrin molecules from adjacent foot processes reach out and join (dimerize), forming a zipper-like structure across the filtration barrier.

 

This interaction is crucial for maintaining the slit diaphragm’s integrity and filtration function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Podocin: Podocin is also vital in the slit diaphragm, but it is not a transmembrane protein with Ig-like domains. Instead, it is associated with the membrane’s inner part, interacting with nephrin to maintain its function.

 

Option C. CD2-associated protein: CD2AP is a scaffolding protein that binds nephrin and podocin, helping with signal transduction and slit diaphragm stability. It is not a transmembrane protein with extracellular Ig domains.

 

Option D. Actin filaments: Actin filaments are part of the podocyte’s cytoskeleton (internal cellular structure), not a transmembrane protein.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nephrin is the key structural protein in the glomerular slit diaphragm, characterized by several extracellular Ig-like domains. It forms connections with nephrin on neighboring podocytes, making it essential to the kidney’s urine filtration barrier.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy Chunnu is recovering from impetigo. One week later, he develops malaise with nausea and a slight fever and passes dark brown urine. Concerned about the same, she is brought to Cerebellum Hospital where laboratory studies show a serum anti-streptolysin O titer of 1:1024. Which of the following is the most likely outcome of his renal disease?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. B. Complete recovery

questions.stem: A 5-year-old male presents with a one-month history of progressive lower extremity edema and fatigue. On physical examination, you notice periorbital swelling, abdominal distension, and decreased breath sounds at the lung bases. Laboratory results show proteinuria (6.8 g/day), hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin 2.5 g/dL), and hyperlipidemia). Renal ultrasound reveals normal-sized kidneys with increased echogenicity. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. Which of the following immunofluorescence findings is most consistent with this patient's diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Linear IgG deposits along the glomerular basement membrane

options.label: B
options.text: Granular IgG deposits in the mesangium and along capillary walls

options.label: D
options.text: Starry-sky appearance due to subepithelial humps

questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. Negative immunofluorescence

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had a fever and chills accompanied by right flank pain for the past 3 days. Microscopic examination of the urine shows many WBCs and WBC casts. Which of the following is the most useful test to obtain on this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Urine culture

 

This 19-year-old woman presents with:

 

  • Fever and chills
  • Right flank pain
  • WBCs and WBC casts in urine

 

These findings are classic for acute pyelonephritis, a bacterial infection of the kidney.

 

Why urine culture is most useful:

 

  • Urine culture confirms the presence and identity of the causative organism (e.g., E. coli most commonly).
  • It also helps in determining antibiotic sensitivity → guides appropriate treatment.
  • Especially useful in complicated or recurrent urinary tract infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Antinuclear antibody (ANA): Used to assess for autoimmune diseases like lupus nephritis, not useful for diagnosing infection.

 

Option B. Renal biopsy: Invasive and unnecessary in suspected pyelonephritis; reserved for unclear diagnosis or non-responsive glomerular diseases.

 

Option C. Plasma renin: Related to blood pressure regulation and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)—not relevant here.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has polyuria for the past year. She has had a high fever for the past 3 days. A renal ultrasound scan shows an enlarged right kidney with pelvic and calyceal enlargement and cortical thinning; the left kidney appears normal. A right-sided nephrectomy is performed, and grossly there are large U-shaped scars at the poles with underlying blunted calyces. Microscopic examination shows inflammatory infiltrates extending from the medulla to the cortex, with tubular destruction and extensive interstitial fibrosis. Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils are abundant. Which of the following underlying conditions is most likely to produce these findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Vesicoureteral reflux

questions.stem: A second-year student is examining a slide of the renal tissue. He observes fibrinoid necrosis in the same and presence of “onion peel appearance” of the blood vessel. The likely slide is of which of the following pathologies?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis  

 

Key findings:

 

  • Fibrinoid necrosis
  • Onion-skin or onion peel appearance of the vessel wall
  • These are classic histological features of hyperplastic arteriosclerosis, often seen in the context of malignant hypertension.

 

Histological details:

 

  • Fibrinoid necrosis:
    • Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes in the vessel wall.
    • Suggests severe vascular injury, seen in malignant hypertension or vasculitis.
    • Onion-skin appearance:
    • Concentric, laminated thickening of arteriolar walls due to proliferation of smooth muscle cells and reduplication of basement membrane.
    • Seen in hyperplastic arteriosclerosis, commonly in malignant hypertension.

 

 

Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (onion-skinning) causing luminal obliteration (arrow) (periodic acid-Schiff stain)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyaline degeneration:

 

  • Seen in benign hypertension or diabetes.
  • Characterized by hyaline (pink, glassy) thickening of vessel walls, not onion-skin.

 

 

Hyaline arteriolosclerosis. The arteriolar wall is thickened with increased protein deposition (hyalinized), and the lumen is markedly narrowed.

 

Option C. Glomerulosclerosis:

 

  • Refers to scarring of the glomerulus.
  • May be seen in diabetic nephropathy or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, but doesn't show onion-skin vessels.

 

Option D. Fibrillary glomerulonephritis:

 

  • Characterized by fibril deposits in the glomerulus (seen with EM).
  • Associated with immune complex deposits, not fibrinoid necrosis or onion-skin vessels.

questions.stem: An adult patient with bilateral renal cystic disease is found to have defects in renal tubular function. Their kidneys are markedly increased in size. They have ciliopathy, with reduced mechano-sensing of tubular fluid flow. Mutations are found in a gene encoding for a protein component of these cilia. What is this protein most likely to be?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D. Polycystin

questions.stem: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome which encompasses Wilms tumor has which of the following additional characteristics?

options.label: A
options.text: Berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hemihypertrophy

 

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is an overgrowth disorder with a predisposition to embryonal tumors, including Wilms tumor. The syndrome is caused by abnormalities in the regulation of imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15.

 

Key features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome:

 

  • Hemihypertrophy (asymmetric overgrowth of one side of the body)
  • Macroglossia (enlarged tongue)
  • Omphalocele or umbilical hernia
  • Visceromegaly (enlarged abdominal organs like liver, kidney, pancreas)
  • Neonatal hypoglycemia
  • Increased risk of embryonal tumors (Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, neuroblastoma)

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis: Associated with adult polycystic kidney disease, not BWS.

 

Option C. Gonadal dysgenesis: Seen in Turner syndrome (45,X), Swyer syndrome, not BWS.

 

Option D. Aniridia: Associated with WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, mental Retardation), not BWS.

questions.stem: What is the most common manifestation of Alport's syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. A. Hematuria

questions.stem: The most consistent and persistent feature of bladder carcinoma is:
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. Painless hematuria
